items.originalTitle: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.author: Joan M. Cook
items.title: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.summary: —Creative Images Lab—Getty Images Hands down, anxiety is the most common mental health issue affecting Americans today. Over 19% of adults in the U.S. meet criteria for an anxiety disorder in any given year. Many often don’t recognize these difficulties, or mistake them for signs of a physical health condition. As a psychologist, I can tell you that worrying is a normal part of life. Occasionally, we all get a little nervous about something. We can fret that we blew a job interview or made a poor impression on a first date. We may feel on edge thinking about a big purchase we need to make and concerned about how we are going to pay for it. Many of us have concerns about money and finances, including how we are going to pay off a mortgage or a big debt. We may experience uneasiness about our relationships, including conflict with a partner or tension with an aging parent. We may be nervous about upcoming deadlines at work or national elections. Other times, our anxiety may be more free-floating, overly intense concerns latching on to any number of things. It’s hard to know how to safely stop the worry cycle, so we often, as humans, over-prepare, try to control a situation, or avoid it altogether. But when anxiety persists and gets worse over time, when it impairs our ability to function on the job or in the classroom, or our ability to connect with others, anxiety becomes problematic and potentially diagnosable. “Anxiety makes people’s lives smaller as they prune all the bits of their lives that lead to anxiety,” says Debra Kaysen , a psychologist and professor at Stanford University. “That works short-term, but long-term steals all the parts of life that give joy.” The great news is that there are effective treatments. Several free, reliable screens can help people do a self-assessment regarding whether they may meet criteria for an anxiety disorder. Though there are a range of anxiety disorders —including generalized anxiety, panic, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive disorder—most have similar underlying causes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) can help to identify and manage the factors that contribute to anxiety. By learning to change unhelpful thought patterns, we can reduce the frequency and intensity of anxious symptoms. We can also learn techniques to regulate our anxiety and help us engage in effective problem-solving. That said, it isn’t always easy to get the help we need. There are a host of barriers, from financial, transportation, and scheduling to stigma, poor access, and limited availability. Anne Marie Albano , a psychologist and professor at Columbia University, has spent decades conducting research on and treating anxiety in children, adolescents, and young adults. Along with her colleagues, Albano developed several effective interventions, including Coaching Approach Behavior and Leading by Modeling (CALM) for families with young children to help them master circumstances that trigger intense discomfort, as well as the Launching Emerging Adults Program (LEAP), which centers on assisting individuals as they work through anxiety during the transition to adulthood. Albano recommends practicing breathing techniques to manage anxiety. “Close your eyes and focus on a quiet or pleasant scene in your mind. Breathe in slowly while counting to three, then pause a second, and then breathe out to the count of three. Breathing slowly and deeply, do this for ten repetitions,” she says. The benefit of this technique is that it’s endlessly versatile. “It’s a quick strategy that once learned, you can use with your eyes open and in any situation. Parents can even do this with their children to teach them belly breathing,” Albano explains. “Adults can use this before meetings or other emotionally challenging situations to regulate themselves and manage not just anxiety but other strong emotions.” In addition to breathing exercises, physical activity is one of the best ways to lessen anxiety for people of all ages. “Getting outside each day, rain or shine, and being physically active and social will build your natural resilience and coping skills. Walking, shooting hoops, yoga, swimming, and especially doing these things with other people will strengthen your physical capacity to manage stress and provide you with social networking and support from others,” Albano lists. Even just 10 or 15 minutes a day can help us feel more calm and capable. Even if, for whatever reason, someone is unable to access formal mental health services, there are things we can do to help ourselves with intense apprehension or looming thoughts of threat, trouble, or catastrophe. In my view, an excellent resource is the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies , an interdisciplinary organization of professionals dedicated to the study of behavioral health. The website has research-based information in English and Spanish about anxiety disorders , treatments , and a therapist directory . Anxiety is common and treatable. The National Institute of Mental Health also offers a wealth of information on anxiety , including free digital brochures and fact sheets , updates from the latest research, and how to find help and support . Help is out there, and if you have persistent anxiety, rest assured you are not alone.

items.author: Ken Ono
items.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
items.summary: I believe human judgment remains essential Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics? In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned. Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions. items.summary: The idea of any guest being hungry, or there not being enough food, is an unspeakable proposition for an Iranian host When most people think of the strait of Hormuz, the warm, tropical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, incredible food isn’t usually the first thing that comes to mind. But it should be, and I would know – it’s where I had one of my most memorable meals. I was visiting Iran, traversing thousands of miles across the country with a local female photographer, mapping out regional specialities for my cookbook The Saffron Tales . Over the course of several months, we cooked and ate in people’s home kitchens, meeting a cross-section of society, from farmers and pharmacists to yoga teachers and restaurant owners, who all shared their favourite foods with us in places as diverse as the snowy mountains outside Tabriz, the rice paddies of the Caspian Sea, and the historic cities of Isfahan and Shiraz. The FBI’s National Crime Information Center is used to connect federal, state and local authorities so that important law enforcement information is available nationwide. NBC News’ Julie Tsirkin reports.

items.originalTitle: Inside the Trump Administration’s Ultra-Processed-Food Fight
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Sources: Anna Moneymaker / Getty; Jc Milhet / AFP
items.title: Inside the Trump Administration’s Ultra-Processed-Food Fight
items.summary: In early August, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. staged a “policy celebration” at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters to give an update on one of his signature initiatives: a new definition of ultra-processed food . Publishing the definition would be the first step toward achieving several “Make America Healthy Again” goals, such as new front-of-package labels to steer consumers away from unhealthy foods and, eventually, a reduction in preventable disease. But even as Kennedy was planning the festivities, a months-long bureaucratic battle was threatening to derail it. Days before the planned event, senior staff at the White House told Kennedy’s team that the definition would need to stay secret because it had not yet cleared a review process at the Office of Management and Budget. That review had become a major point of contention. Some inside the administration wanted more data on the economic effects of policies that could follow from the definition; others insisted that the delay was unnecessary and political. When Kennedy took the stage, flanked by children holding Eat Real Food posters, he could announce only that an announcement was still coming. This dispute over regulatory language has since helped unravel the team that cemented the MAHA-MAGA alliance and has guided Donald Trump for years. Less than two weeks before the midterms, a Kennedy ally named Calley Means quit his job at the White House in protest. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles then mounted a new effort to release the definition before the election, only to have Kennedy pause it. On the same day that Wiles announced her resignation following a poor Republican showing in the midterm election, Means appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast to accuse her of caving to the food industry. Inside the White House, some staff were outraged. One White House official that day called Means a liar and a failure who “confuses his own inability to persuade with others’ malfeasance.” Now, under the new regime of Chief of Staff Stephen Miller—who has long claimed his own special affinity for MAHA—the ultra-processed-food language, a draft of which we obtained, is once again moving forward. According to several people with knowledge of the plan, HHS has been preparing again for a long-awaited release of the definition, which is expected as soon as next week. (When asked for comment, HHS directed us to the White House, which sent a statement that listed past MAHA accomplishments and declared, “Stephen Miller and Secretary Kennedy have been working closely together since day one, and they will continue advancing bipartisan MAHA victories.”) The story of the conflagration at the White House, which involves Trump-administration staff trading accusations of corruption and incompetence, is based on interviews with eight current and former officials involved in the process, most of whom requested anonymity to describe conversations that occurred behind closed doors. The dispute exposed major divisions within the White House over how far to take Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again agenda. Now the future of the UPF definition will signal whether the alliance between MAGA and MAHA can survive. The government’s proposed definition of ultra-processed food has remained largely unchanged since a team led by then-Food and Drug Commissioner Marty Makary first drafted it, in the summer of 2025, according to people close to the process. In about 200 words, it classifies as ultra-processed any food or drink containing a chemical preservative, artificial color, added flavor, or low- or no-calorie sweetener such as stevia and aspartame. Additives intended to thicken foods or otherwise alter their texture, such as guar gum and sodium alginate, will also land a food on the UPF list. The definition relies heavily on existing federal regulations that spell out what, exactly, qualifies as a color, sweetener, or other additive. It excludes infant formula, dietary supplements, and foods that qualify as “healthy” under an FDA standard that sets limits on added sugar, sodium, and saturated fat. (Those products also must contain minimum amounts of healthy ingredients such as fruit and whole grains.) Even with those exceptions, experts we spoke with said, the definition of an ultra-processed food would likely cover most packaged products on grocery-store shelves—not just classic junk food, like cheese-filled pretzel bites, but also many flavored yogurts, instant oatmeals, and protein bars. Most packaged breads, which contain additives that prevent mold and maintain softness, would go on the list too. That’s a frightening proposition to the food industry. The Consumer Brands Association, which represents some of the country’s largest food and beverage manufacturers, including PepsiCo and Tyson Foods, argues that the suspected harms of UPFs—obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer—have not been confirmed by strong scientific evidence. It’s true that the science on UPFs, including which ingredients or processes might make them unhealthy, remains unsettled. But nutrition experts told us that enough evidence links them to poor health outcomes that consumers should be warned. That prospect—that the UPF definition will lead to new regulations and legal actions—has been the crux of the fight inside the administration. Kennedy has advocated for new front-of-package UPF labeling that would be similar to cigarette warnings. The Consumer Brands Association has argued that such a requirement would place an undue burden on food manufacturers. The association has touted a recent study by University of Chicago economists predicting that a mandatory label would prompt food companies to spend billions to reformulate their products, raising the average household’s annual grocery bill by $60. But several nutrition experts we spoke with questioned the study’s assumptions. Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutritional epidemiologist, told us that companies are “reformulating and changing their packaging all the time” and still manage to bring in billions in profit. In fact, some companies have done so recently as part of Kennedy’s push to remove artificial dyes from the American food supply. So far General Mills has voluntarily dropped them from cereals sold in the United States, and Kellogg says it plans to ship reformulated Froot Loops and Apple Jacks by year’s end. Food companies are also concerned that a federal definition might be used in litigation. In the past two years, consumers, as well as the city of San Francisco, have sued major food companies over alleged harmful health effects, and advocates hope that a new definition could make their cases more credible. One attorney, John Morgan of Morgan & Morgan, has been especially active in these suits; his firm previously collaborated with Kennedy on an environmental case and maintained a working relationship with him until he became health secretary. That connection “does raise questions in our mind” about Kennedy’s motivations, Rhonda Bentz, a spokesperson for the Consumer Brands Association, told us. Morgan told us that he doesn’t need a new federal definition to help him make a case against food companies, but did not rule out incorporating one. “Their defense is always the same one,” he told us. “It’s deny, delay, deny, delay.” Given how vehemently the food industry opposes these measures, some drama over a government UPF definition was inevitable. But at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the two people at the center of the fight nonetheless believed that they could find a solution. Besides Trump and Kennedy, Means and Wiles were the most significant players in the unlikely merger of MAHA and MAGA. Wiles had reached out to Means in 2023 after reading his ideas about public-health reform, and Means first connected Kennedy to Trump. In the weeks that followed, Wiles led the negotiations to merge the Kennedy and Trump campaigns. “Susie Wiles is the best choice of chief of staff for MAHA,” Means posted on X in November 2024, when she was named to the post. In 2025, Wiles green-lighted an aggressive series of reports and announcements in which Kennedy put forward his plans to define ultra-processed food, redesign the food pyramid, and review school and military meals. But Wiles also established a policy process that rankled Means and his allies, allowing different Cabinet departments—as well as lobbyists and industry leaders—to weigh in on changes. “Susie wanted to get to yes, but we had to do it in a way that doesn’t endanger the U.S. food supply,” a government official involved in the policy discussions told us. Means came to believe that the process was just an excuse for further delay, he told us. “The problem with Susie’s leadership was there was no process, and special-interest phone calls were able to delay or kill key priorities that the president ran on,” he said. (Wiles declined to comment for this article.) Kennedy’s staff frequently clashed with farmers, food producers, and Department of Agriculture staff. As we reported in July , MAHA activists inside and outside the administration had become especially frustrated with Heidi Overton, a medical doctor and White House policy adviser, who often slowed down health-policy changes to refine them. Wiles vocally defended Overton and the process at the time, telling us that the White House was focused on making sure “things are correct, legally durable, done with policy consistency.” (Trump nominated Overton to be FDA commissioner in August, but withdrew that nomination earlier this week.) By late last summer, officials at HHS believed that the UPF definition was ready to go. But at an interagency gathering this July, Means was peppered with questions about what the new definition would mean for food prices and the liability of food producers, as well as whether it would be vulnerable to legal challenge, according to people familiar with the meeting. For his part, Means warned other officials that they would be seen as catering to industry interests if they did not embrace the definition, which had then been circulating inside the administration for about nine months. Wiles’s team later insisted that the concerns raised at the meeting had not been addressed. The fact that Republicans were being hammered in campaigns across the country for the rising costs of food also weighed on the White House. Backers of the UPF definition viewed such complaints as stonewalling and were concerned that the delay would endanger their ability to get regulations such as new food labels in place before the end of Trump’s term. “It was two pages,” another person involved in the policy discussions told us. “The idea that you have to do some complex policy process for a two-page proposal is laughable.” Means told us that hundreds of meetings were held to discuss the definition, and he stopped believing that the White House would release one before the election. So he quit. When Means appeared on Rogan’s podcast, he alleged that Wiles had told him that she had concerns about a separate MAHA-coded effort—this one to regulate additives—because Republicans needed money from the sugar industry for the midterms. Allies of Wiles denied that she ever said this, and people who worked with her pointed out that the sugar industry ranked low among top donors to Republican election efforts. The day after his Rogan appearance, Means invited Wiles to sue him. After Means left the White House, Wiles and Kennedy started working again to release the UPF definition so that it could receive public comment before being finalized next year. In the week before the election, the White House and Wiles cleared a version of the definition, including a preamble specifying that it should not yet be used in litigation or for shaping legislation. Then, just days before the election, Kennedy decided that the process was too rushed and opted to wait to announce the language until after the election. The definition that is set to be released now is not expected to be materially different, people involved in the process told us. Kennedy has also carefully kept some distance from the controversy. After Means denounced Wiles as corrupt, Kennedy praised her “inspiring leadership and wisdom” in a post on social media. Trump—who has at times sounded even more aggressive than Kennedy on some MAHA issues, especially those related to childhood vaccines—has remained silent. The White House has not yet announced whether the president will be involved in the release of the new ultra-processed-food standards. Following Means’s departure and the Republicans’ midterms disaster, some pundits were ready to write off MAHA entirely. The unlikely coalition appeared to be fraying, its supporters were demoralized, and most of the candidates backed by its political-action committee lost their race. But MAHA’s obituary may turn out to be premature. A federal UPF definition would be Kennedy’s most tangible win yet, and a sign that MAHA might still have some life left. Assuming, that is, it finally gets published.

items.originalTitle: My Apology to American Democracy
items.author: Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic. Source: Sarah Silbiger / Bloomberg /
items.title: My Apology to American Democracy
items.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. A fter any election, it’s natural to hunt for results that prove you were right all along. Landslides in particular provide the winners with ample evidence to sustain just about every prior position. At the moment, Democrats are engaged in a familiar argument over which faction, the progressives or the moderates, can claim responsibility for the party’s remarkable new majority. If you support Medicare for All, you’ll point to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan. If you’re a skeptic, Roy Cooper of North Carolina won the election’s biggest blowout for a flipped Senate seat. If you want to retire the culture war, look at Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico in Texas. If you thought the race was about Palestine and trans issues, Victoria Broderick just became Tennessee’s first queer member-elect of Congress. Latinos, independents, southern Black women, men under 30, the white working class: bragging rights for all. But it might be more useful to search for what you got wrong. Views that are exploded by subsequent events have a way of disappearing from the mind, making it easy to forget you ever held them in the first place, and creating an illusion that your political wishes always accord with reality. We’re all prone to squeezing facts into the shape of narratives we carry in our heads and ignoring facts that undermine them. These mental habits contribute to a culture of total vindication and no compromise. They also make it difficult to understand present events or predict future ones. Last year, I wrote that America was becoming an authoritarian state. There were grounds for believing it. Think back to the country that America seemed to have become. President Trump ruled with almost no checks on his power. The Supreme Court offered little resistance and Congress none, as if the Constitution had been suspended and the entire federal government had come under the control of one man. The civil service had been gutted, independent agencies neutered, and the Justice Department warped into the president’s personal tool for rewarding friends, punishing enemies, and enriching himself. Long-standing norms of language, behavior, and probity collapsed daily. Elites in business, media, academia, and law lay supine before Trump’s demands for fealty and lucre. After returning to power a man who had tried to nullify democracy, the public seemed entirely passive: content, checked out, or too stunned to react. [ Listen: Autocracy in America ] Remember the fear, the confusion turning to panic. Masked gunmen swept through American neighborhoods, foreigners stayed away from American airports, and international students began to disappear from American universities. After Charlie Kirk’s murder, the White House set out to purge his detractors, and Stephen Miller warned the enemies of goodness—perhaps half the country—that they had awakened a dragon. In red towns, regime critics lowered their voices. In blue cities, families talked seriously about the possibility of moving to another country. Famous figures in the resistance began to leave , while some people I knew tried to parlay a deceased grandparent into a foreign passport and had their children apply to overseas colleges. How could you raise kids here? What if the previous election had returned to power a president who would make sure there would never be another? No one wanted to be the fool who waited too long to get out. But how would you know when it was too late? Having no experience with these dilemmas, we looked to history for guidance. The spirit of the moment was captured in a recent translation of The Oppermanns , written in 1933 by the German Jewish novelist Lion Feuchtwanger, who had the foresight to flee as soon as Hitler came to power. The lesson seemed to be: Get out while you still can. In its annual democracy index for 2025, Freedom House gave the United States its lowest score ever—on par with South Africa and below Panama. Political minds debated what to call this radical deformation of democracy: right-wing populist, illiberal, authoritarian, patrimonialist—even fascist. I wrote an article about this ominous state of affairs with the title “ America’s Zombie Democracy .” Now a free election has delivered an overwhelming rebuke to Trump and his rule. What kind of fascist allows that to happen? I f I were to summarize the flaws in my own thinking, I would say that I overrated Trump’s competence as a dictator, and I underrated the resilience of American democracy. “I don’t think that people were wrong to be worried, and I don’t think the threat is over,” Lawrence Norden, an election-security expert at the Brennan Center for Justice, told me. “I do think maybe some people underestimated the ability to fight back.” Trump wants to rule as a fascist. His governing style emulates the classic features of fascism: cult of the leader, nationalist and xenophobic rhetoric, glorification of the “real” people, demonization of minorities and political opponents, relish for violence, a blizzard of propaganda and lies. Last January, at what was probably the peak of his power following the raid on Venezuela, he declared that only “my own morality, my own mind,” could stop him from doing anything he wanted around the world. But Trump is too shallow, undisciplined, and selfish to lead a great movement with an idealistic vision of the state that can outlive him. He has spent much of his second term distracted by vanity construction projects and self-enrichment schemes. His lifelong attraction to crassly beautiful women has become, in his less priapic ninth decade, an attraction to crassly rich men—Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, Jensen Huang. Trump, his family, and his circle have shown their contempt for the MAGA base by descending into unprecedented depths of corruption at a time of rising prices and interest rates. A competent dictator wouldn’t lose touch with the people whose voice he claims to be. He wouldn’t allow his regime to take the place of the arrogant elites who had served as foils on his way to power. He wouldn’t keep harping on his new ballroom. Trump is a failed fascist. Just as Americans who have known no system other than liberal democracy struggle to imagine its downfall, to understand an authoritarian American president, we tried to compare him to analogues past and present. When Trump was first elected, in 2016, a friend said, “We have to hope he’s Berlusconi, not Mussolini.” Trump is both, and the mix of showman and strongman makes him harder to predict than either one separately. It’s intellectually more straightforward to think of him in the mold of a figure like Vladimir Putin than, say, Alberto Fujimori. It’s also emotionally more satisfying: The lines are clear; the stakes couldn’t be higher; a great battle is on. When, a year ago, I wrote the words “We are living in an authoritarian state,” I felt a shudder of fear and gloom, but also, unmistakably, of excitement. I thought that in his second term Trump would focus single-mindedly on keeping and using power. In the first year he did, and many of us worried that in the second year he might rig or annul the midterms. This wasn’t a far-fetched concern: Trump tried to change voting rules, disqualify registered voters, intimidate election officials with threats of criminal charges, mobilize the Justice Department to challenge results. With election denialists holding key state offices and rogue immigration agents possibly guarding the polls, Trump could keep an irrevocably gerrymandered Congress Republican and harden MAGA’s lock on power. Then he might find a way to continue as president for a third term or install one of his children in the White House. None of this was a fever dream, but it gave Trump too much credit. As it turned out, the midterms held his attention only fitfully. When courts struck down his executive orders, he didn’t defy them. When people in Minneapolis found the courage to protest the thugs with guns who were terrorizing their neighbors and killing American citizens, Trump backed off. Almost on a whim, he started a ruinous war with Iran. While his popularity sank, he went about relining the Reflecting Pool, changing the interior design of the White House ballroom, and enlarging plans for the Triumphal Arch. He spent a lot of time organizing garish celebrations of America’s 250th birthday, claiming it as his own. Actually governing the country hardly seemed to interest him. His appearances in the fall campaign grew more and more bizarre—no one remembers anything from those speeches except a few obscene insults and a peculiar fixation on a Republican senator’s buttocks. Historical analogies pointed to the Roman emperor Caligula. And when, on November 3, the voters gave a shattering blow to Trump and his movement—a loss too big to rig or overturn—his initial response was a shrug. After all, his name wasn’t on the ballot. Within the gilded walls of his own mind, he remained undiminished. Whereas Trump proved unequal to the demands of holding autocratic power, American democracy in 2026 showed a resilience that seemed to have disappeared in 2025. A year ago I thought that little stood between Trump and the consolidation of authoritarian rule. The institutions were hollow and the elites spineless. But this year two of those institutions made sure that the public would have a say: the federal courts and the state and local election system. Almost every attempt by the administration to change voting rules, interfere with election officials, and manipulate the vote count was blocked by the courts, including, in at least one case, the Supreme Court. Election officials around the country resisted the administration’s efforts to intimidate them. Norden, of the Brennan Center, said, “We are lucky that we have a very decentralized election system in the U.S., and the states and civil society were able to take advantage of that to be ready for the assault.” So the people would get a chance to speak. [ Read: How Americans defeated an autocrat-in-waiting ] Despite Trump’s abysmal ratings, I hadn’t forgotten that this electorate returned him to power after he had summoned a mob to try to stop the peaceful transition of power for the first time since the Civil War. Nothing has ever shaken my faith in my compatriots like a presidential election in which the price of eggs mattered more than the fate of democracy. The midterms showed that democracy still matters to most Americans—fitfully, like Trump’s interest in ruling, and not necessarily as a set of abstract concepts called separation of powers , rule of law , and independent judiciary , but in a more visceral way, as a sense of fairness and common decency. Few Americans cared about the destruction of foreign aid by a private citizen who happens to be the richest man in the world. The firing of inspectors general across the federal government aroused little protest. But this didn’t mean that the public had entirely lost its self-respect. Americans who voted for Trump three times were still capable of turning against him. Throughout the year, offense at Trump’s callous excesses slowly rose until it became unstoppable. His greatest mistake was thinking that his spectacular corruption would be of no concern to ordinary people, as if grift on a grand scale came with the divine right to rule. Americans are more likely to ignore abuses of power when times are good. But in a year when health premiums along with the price of gas and diesel spiked, Trump’s gold ballroom and Qatari jet affronted a people who apparently still believe that they are their own masters in a self-governing republic. They just had to be reminded. It was better to exaggerate than underrate Trump’s ability to bring 250 years of democracy to an end. For a distracted and amnesiac people, sleepwalking into authoritarianism remains a risk; the vigilance aroused by Trump’s lawless presidency should be our constant state. But those 250 years have left expectations and habits in American minds that, though they might disappear for a time, are not easily killed.

Photo by Steve James/Addison This story by Marin Howell was first published in the Addison Independent on Nov. 12, 2026. Favorable weather made for an abundant apple season at orchards around Addison County this fall. With the season winding down — or already wrapped up at some spots — local growers reported plentiful crops and expressed gratitude for community members’ support. “It was wonderful,” Kathleen Stine, of Monkton’s Stine Orchard, said of the season. “In the beginning there were some important days that were rainy, but after that it was a gorgeous season. The fruit was plentiful, the doughnuts never stopped, and the cookies never stopped.” Stine and her husband, Aaron, co-own Stine Orchard, where they grow over 20 varieties of apples, along with pears and plums. Kathleen Stine said all of the orchard’s apple varieties fared well this year. “People’s favorites are typically (McIntosh) and Honeycrisps, but we have some cult followings for the Northern Spy, for example,” she said. As of early November, Stine Orchard had closed for the season but planned to be open on select Saturdays for doughnuts, with community members able to pick from what’s left on the trees for 50 cents per pound. The orchard team was also busy gearing up for Thanksgiving, with orders coming in for goods like pies and cider doughnuts and a pickup day planned for the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Vergennes area This year’s season has also wrapped up at Woodman Hill Orchard in Ferrisburgh. Run by Steph Lowe and Rob Rogers, the orchard grows several varieties of apples at 175 Plank Road just outside Vergennes. The orchard’s season went well overall, according to Rogers and Lowe. “It was a successful harvest, we made mountains of doughnuts and hosted many field trips, which is always such a joy,” they told the Independent. “It’s an intense two months, but we feel very fulfilled … and ready for a break!” They noted how this year’s weather made for a positive pick-your-own season. “It was a bit dry to start but we had good rain earlier this summer so the apple quality didn’t suffer,” they said. “We were lucky that the cold nights in October didn’t get cold enough to bring apple picking to an end and we were able to sell through the end of the month. It was a good, long picking season this year.” An orchard visitor has an abundance of options to choose from while picking Empire apples at Woodman Hill Orchard in Ferrisburgh. The orchard had a successful harvest this year, echoing other area growers in reporting a good apple crop and positive pick-your-own season. items.originalTitle: Nvidia’s next CEO must lead a supervised international business—amid the ‘complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium,’ investor says
items.author: Joshua Hong
items.title: Nvidia’s next CEO must lead a supervised international business—amid the ‘complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium,’ investor says
items.summary: Following the ouster of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, the company’s next chief executive will inherit a company facing a fundamentally different set of challenges than the ones that once propelled it to become the world’s most valuable company. Beyond sustaining demand for its AI chips, the next leader needs to navigate intensifying U.S. export restrictions, investigations into the company’s China business and scrutiny of its financial arrangements. That’s according to Nvidia investor Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial—the parent company of REX Shares, which oversees $8.5 billion in assets under management. “The bigger problem going forward isn’t actually who sits in the CEO chair. It is the Chinese chip access,” he told Fortune via email. For years, U.S. restrictions sought to limit China’s ability to purchase Nvidia’s most powerful processors. But Huang’s affair with an executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed raised concerns about Chinese companies accessing restricted hardware. The Trump administration is now moving to plug those gaps. Last Sunday, the federal government announced a rule to close a loophole that allowed remote access to advanced AI chips and servers via overseas data centers. And on Friday, President Donald Trump said he wanted to prevent American companies from building data centers overseas. “Whoever runs Nvidia next will inherit a narrower, more closely supervised international business and the complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium that comes with it,” Birmingham said. The company’s latest earnings demonstrate how big its commercial momentum remained following its news spiral. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for Q3 2026, a 103% increase from a year earlier. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion, accounting for approximately 93% of total revenue. But Birmingham argued that the earnings are becoming less important than what management says about future demand, pricing power and the sustainability of the AI investment cycle. A company under heavy investigation The California attorney general’s office subpoenaed Nvidia as part of an investigation into whether the company or Huang enabled China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information—or misled investors about the associated risks. The SEC is also investigating the company over whether the company misled investors in its public disclosures, according to the New York Post . The civil probe comes amid questions from officials on whether Nvidia knew about its potential diversion of chips to China and whether its disclosures adequately addressed the risks. Trump has also said the FBI is investigating Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang and any ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Congress will join in the scrutiny too. Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before three House committees about the company’s potential role in allowing Chinese entities to access advanced American chips. Lawmakers will probe the Commerce Department’s role after the House Foreign Affairs Committee disclosed on Thursday that the Commerce Department had approved 879,868 advanced semiconductor shipments to Chinese companies across 21 license applications between December 2025 and May 2026. There’s also an AI infrastructure problem Export restrictions are also just one piece of the puzzle Nvidia needs to solve. The company has to contend with the financial structure supporting unprecedented expansion of AI infrastructure, according to Birmingham. The concern is that demand for Nvidia’s processors are tied to the ability of hyperscalers and smaller cloud providers to finance enormous data center investments. But that creates a fragile relationship between Nvidia’s hardware sales and the financial health of its customers, Birmingham said. “Given the AI ecosystem is being heavily supported by vendor financing and debt markets, the potential for a telecom style bust is significant,” he warned. Birmingham said Nvidia’s August announcement that it intended to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital through partnerships with major financial institutions—including BlackRock , Goldman Sachs , KKR and others—to finance AI infrastructure was concerning. He said the commitments were “clear” they were “made exclusively by Huang,” meaning investors would need clarity about whether the company intends to maintain them. In its latest quarterly filing, Nvidia disclosed that the financing platforms were still preliminary arrangements that might not result in definitive agreements. The company outlined that it could provide limited residual-value support for specific projects at its discretion. Unlike established hyperscalers, neocloud providers have less flexibility to absorb rising hardware and financing costs, Birmingham said. “They need near-perfect utilization to stay profitable,” he added. “In general, they can only pass along higher costs to new contracts, and only when compute stays scarce.” This means if demand weakens, neocloud providers could find themselves paying for expensive computing infrastructure without being able to generate the revenue to service their debt. “Investors are assessing whether the AI supply cycle is running too hot, and if a break point in compute demand will force a pullback in datacenter build out that becomes self-reinforcing across the system,” he explained. items.originalTitle: I am SNL’s ‘sister.’ caregiving is an act of love, but love isn’t a care plan
items.author: Tatyana Zlotsky
items.title: I am SNL’s ‘sister.’ caregiving is an act of love, but love isn’t a care plan
items.summary: The Saturday Night Live ’s “Sister” sketch struck a chord with families across the nation. Why? Because they saw themselves in the story. Let’s face it: when an aging parent needs care, it’s often the women, the “Sisters”, who step up and take on the responsibility. I’m grateful to SNL for bringing this topic forward. Sometimes humor opens the door to a conversation we have been avoiding. But recognizing the problem is only the beginning. We have to change what we expect from the women in our families. For me, watching the video was painful and hit very close to home. And the many texts I received afterward, as CEO of A Place for Mom, were even more heartbreaking. I am the sister. I know firsthand what that responsibility feels like because my mom and I cared for my incredible grandparents for nearly 20 years. I came to the United States as a teenager and helped my grandparents navigate senior care while still learning the system myself. I know what it means to feel tremendous guilt, worry about people you love, and not know where to turn. For 25 years, we have been helping families navigate one of life’s most difficult and emotional journeys: finding care for an aging loved one. More than 2.3 million families have turned to us for support, and approximately 40% of family caregivers we serve are daughters, daughter-in-laws, nieces and sisters-in-law. In fact, more than two-thirds of the people that reach out are women. Once we connect with the family, our goal is to help them understand where to start, make sense of their options, navigate difficult decisions, and feel more confident about what comes next. When families are ready to explore care, we connect them with providers across our network of more than 15,000 senior living communities and home care agencies, helping them find options that align with their individual needs, preferences, and budgets. The service we provide is at no cost to families as we are paid by our provider network. Over the past seven years at the company, I’ve also witnessed firsthand the uncertainty, guilt, and fear that so many of the families we support experience. When Mom or Dad falls, who gets the call? Who manages medications, makes appointments, and researches care options? Nationally, women account for 61% of unpaid caregivers, according to AARP. And once she starts, everyone assumes she will keep doing it. And she does. In A Place for Mom’s 2026 Women and Caregiving report, we found that women caregivers report stress, guilt, and overwhelm more often than men, and 53% have trouble sleeping at least once a week. They also give up more of what they earn: 33% of household income, compared with 29% for men, from households already bringing in about $15,000 less. We have somehow talked ourselves into the idea that the more a woman sacrifices, the more we should praise her. She steps back from work. Puts off her own appointments. We tell her how strong she is. We should be asking what support she needs and taking responsibility for providing it. Two things need to change. First, caregiving has to be a family responsibility. Brothers, sons, and other family members need to be involved. Many already are. We need more. Make the appointment and handle the follow-up. Research the care options. Commit to regular support. “Tell me what you need” still leaves her responsible for figuring it out and assigning it. Every person’s contribution will look different. Distance, finances, health, and work matter. Discuss those realities instead of assuming one person will cover everything. Second, we have to stop treating sacrifice and suffering as proof of love. You are not a better daughter because you are losing income or neglecting your health. Getting support does not mean you love your parents less. This holiday season, my wish is that families have an honest conversation about what help Mom or Dad needs and who will take responsibility. An easy way to start is by discussing needs, expectations, and what each person can contribute. Importantly, the conversation needs to be candid, specific, and have clear follow-through. And please, don’t leave it to “Sister” to organize that, too. Siblings can start together, then bring Mom or Dad into the conversation, with their preferences at the center of the plan. Having a sister is a gift, not a senior care strategy. To our sisters: We see you. You deserve support and time to be a daughter or sister, not always the caregiver. To everyone counting on her: Take responsibility for something she can stop carrying. items.originalTitle: Americans are paying $290 to meet strangers as friendship apps spread to more than 200 cities
items.author: Michaela Herbst
items.title: Americans are paying $290 to meet strangers as friendship apps spread to more than 200 cities
items.summary: Startups are betting on America’s loneliness epidemic, and Americans are buying in. Apps such as 222, Real Roots, and Timeleft are turning friend-matching events into a growing consumer market, and some users pay hundreds of dollars to make new friends offline. Alexandra Pitzer paid $290 through Real Roots last year to meet a group of strangers, The New York Times reported . She had just moved from Nashville to Honolulu for her husband’s Army job and was looking for connection. The app placed her at a brewery with eight other women. “I can see most of them being lifelong friends,” Pitzer told the Times . “We have a genuine connection.” The business is working, at least for now: each of the three companies brings in millions of dollars in revenue a year, according to the Times . But the model carries an unusual tension. The better it works, the less its customers may need it. How 222 turned backyard dinners into a venture-backed startup These companies are tapping into demand for in-person connection at a time when many people struggle to build relationships in a digital age. Rather than meeting people the old-fashioned way, users are matched with strangers based on shared interests and personality, then sent to curated events. 222 began as a college research project. Its co-founders later started hosting dinners in their backyard, and the project became a full-time business in 2023, according to the Times . The company has since raised $13.7 million in venture capital, according to Business Insider , including $10.1 million in 2025. It uses machine-learning models trained on users’ feedback after each meetup to decide who should meet whom. “I think our generation craves the in-real-life environment of meeting each other in a more intimate setting, without digital preconceptions,” Arman Roshannai, one of 222’s co-founders, told the Times . 222 charges $22 a month to match users and curate events, before the cost of the activity itself, such as a yoga class or a meal. Interested in dinner and collage-making? That will be $38, not including food and drinks. The company now operates in 21 cities, employs 27 people and hosts at least one experience a day. Its co-founders told the Times that revenue tripled last year and is on track to quadruple this year, into the high seven figures. Competitors are scaling, too. Real Roots, which coordinates activities for groups of women, is in 120 cities, while Timeleft, which matches strangers for dinners, is in more than 200. Newer entrants keep arriving, including the professional-networking app Clockout, whose founder raised $3.5 million to help Gen Z feel less alone . All of them are competing for users who want a genuine relationship beyond social media. Ironically, building these friendships starts with an app. The demand behind the boom About 21% of U.S. adults reported feeling lonely in a May 2024 survey by Making Caring Common, a project of the Harvard Graduate School of Education . Among those lonely adults, 81% reported anxiety or depression. Sixty-five percent of lonely respondents said they felt fundamentally disconnected from others or the world. And when all respondents were asked what contributes to loneliness in America, technology topped the list, cited by 73%. Others pointed to families not spending enough time together, people working too much and mental health challenges that strain relationships. Founders in the space argue that this gap is a market in its own right. As the co-founder of group-travel startup WeRoad argued in a Fortune commentary , people who haven’t found meaningful connection online are now willing to pay for it in person. Can friendship be a repeat purchase? Turning friendship into a business doesn’t guarantee meaningful connections. Some users have complained on social media that they didn’t click with their group or that the experiences felt awkward and forced, the Times reported. There is also a larger question about the sustainability of the business model. If the product works and customers develop genuine friendships, they may no longer need the service. That creates an unusual challenge for companies built around solving loneliness. Their success hinges on helping people establish relationships, and every relationship that sticks could mean one fewer customer coming back. The companies appear to be designing around that problem. If a Real Roots group gets along, its members can pay the company to keep arranging meetups for the same group in the weeks that follow. Business Insider reported that 222 is building tools that help users plan their next meetup together and says its users are split roughly evenly between those looking for friends and those open to romance. For investors, the question isn’t simply whether Americans will pay to make friends. It is whether friendship can be a durable business without turning human connection into a subscription. items.author: K. Fiegenbaum
items.title: Cabot to hold January referendum on closing its high school
items.summary: Cabot School on November 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger " data-large-file="https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School.jpg" /> Cabot School on November 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger " data-large-file="https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School.jpg" src="https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School.jpg" alt="A white, single-story school building with a steeple and a parking lot in the foreground." class="wp-image-659572" srcset="https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School.jpg 1200w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-300x225.jpg 300w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-125x94.jpg 125w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-768x576.jpg 768w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-800x600.jpg?crop=1 800w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-600x450.jpg?crop=1 600w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-400x300.jpg?crop=1 400w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-200x150.jpg?crop=1 200w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-1024x768.jpg 1024w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-780x585.jpg 780w, https://vtdigger.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Cabot-School-706x530.jpg 706w" sizes="(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1200px" /> Cabot School on November 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger In March, the Cabot School board of directors got some surprising news. Full-time high school attendance was unexpectedly going to drop by nearly 30% for the upcoming school year, with fewer than 25 students attending the small preK-12 school’s upper grades. The rest, 22 high school age students, are either attending early college , other public or independent high schools via the state’s regional high school choice program or are part-time at Cabot’s high school and part-time in career and technical education programs. That news, along with the state’s nascent district merger process , led the board to conclude unanimously in July that the high school is “not sustainable” with so few students, according to school board member Ellen Cairns. While closing the school likely will not save money or reduce the tax rate, the board says sending students elsewhere would increase academic and social opportunities for them. On Jan. 6, Cabot voters are set to decide whether to close their high school next June and tuition the remaining students out to the public high school or independent school of their choice come next fall. Cabot School would continue to operate its preK-8 grades. If the majority of the town’s approximately 1,200 voters do not support the closure, then the school board would pursue a merger with the nearby preK-12 Danville School, Tormey said — a process that would span several years. The board already looked to expedite that option with Danville, but found that a fast-tracked merger was not possible. Cabot’s vote comes as small schools in Vermont are under increased pressure to make changes and curb costs. Act 170 , passed this spring, outlines a process for districts and supervisory unions to consider merging with each other to save on administrative and maintenance costs. Act 73 , passed in 2025, aims to shift school budgeting decisions away from districts and to the state. The law also established class size minimums. Cabot’s high school, which focuses on project-based learning , has survived four community-petitioned votes about its existence over the past 14 years. However, this will be the first vote brought by the school board itself, which has spent much time and effort over the past decade to research and educate the community about its options. “We’re getting to the point where I think the status quo is not something we’re looking forward to maintaining,” Tormey, who has been on the school board since 2004, said earlier this month. The board is not taking a position on the question of closing the high school versus pursuing a merger. “I think it’s important at this point to check in with the community,” the school board chair said. The cost of sending Cabot’s high school students to other schools next year would be slightly more than the savings from staff reductions and reduced facilities costs related to closing the high school, preliminary estimates from the school administration show. The actual cost would depend on tuition costs for the schools chosen by Cabot’s high school students. Announced tuition rates for next school year at nearby high schools, including the historic independent schools Lyndon Institute and St. Johnsbury Academy, range from $19,500 to $26,588 per student. The cost would also depend on how many members of Cabot’s currently homeschooled community might decide to take advantage of future high school choice. The cost of a merger with Danville School — located about 20 minutes away from Cabot School — is uncertain, though transportation to the merged school would be provided for all students. In a school choice scenario, transportation is typically up to the student and their family. While Tormey says the higher-than-usual number of students taking advantage of opportunities outside of the high school this year is a compliment to their abilities and education, he also acknowledges a “very, very unusual set of circumstances” in school leadership that may have led to it. In the spring of 2024, Cabot residents voted to keep the high school open by a 367-239 margin. Following that vote, the school board hired a new principal — Jennifer Blake — to lead Cabot School, school board member Cairns wrote in this month’s edition of the Cabot Chronicle . Blake “led some popular changes at the school,” and some students who had attended other schools or were homeschooled enrolled in the high school, Cairns wrote, improving numbers and morale. However, after just a year, Blake resigned for “personal and professional reasons,” she wrote in her letter of resignation, and two part-time interim principals led Cabot School last year. The school board terminated the contract of the principal hired for this year, Darin Carney, just two weeks prior to the start of the school year. “Being a principal at a K-12 building is always a challenge,” said Caledonia Central Supervisory Union Superintendent Matt Foster, who oversees Cabot as well as Danville, Twinfield, Walden, Waterford, Peacham and Barnet schools. “The Vermont political environment around closures adds to the difficulty of attracting and retaining good building administrators,” Foster wrote in an email earlier this month. READ MORE A new principal, Paul Grimaud, is slated to start this month, and Tormey said that all are looking forward to having a “much more stable leadership situation at the school.” Grimaud is a longtime educator who most recently was the principal of an American school in the United Arab Emirates. In the meantime, leadership responsibilities at Cabot School have been shared by four Supervisory Union staff who are certified to serve as principal. Initial opinions among community members on closing the high school versus continuing a merger with Danville School have been split. A community survey earlier this fall showed that 58% of the 137 respondents were most supportive of closing the high school and 34% of respondents wanted to continue operating the high school while exploring a merger. A slight majority of the nine current students who responded to the survey, 57%, were supportive of closing the high school and transitioning to school choice. However, the survey has been criticized by community members for not being distributed widely enough and lacking adequate information about the district’s options. “I don’t want to see the high school go,” said Erica Fucello, a Cabot resident who previously served on the school board for a year and a half, in a September meeting . Her three children — a senior participating in early college, a freshman and a third-grader — are very happy at Cabot School, she said. Several community members at the September meeting spoke about the toll that the uncertain future of the high school is having on students and stressed the importance of a clear path forward. Rory Thibault, a former longtime school board member, said that he and his wife spend a lot of time trying to shield his eighth grader from the ongoing discussions. “It’s unavoidable,” he said. “The question of ‘where am I going next year?’ is overwhelming.” The board is working on an updated version of financial projections that will be mailed to all voters in December to inform as many residents as possible about the school’s options. items.originalTitle: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
items.author: Roslyn Henry and Peter Alexander, The Conversation
items.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
items.summary: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses. items.originalTitle: Forget what Randi Weingarten says, school choice didn’t hurt Republicans in midterms
items.title: Forget what Randi Weingarten says, school choice didn’t hurt Republicans in midterms
items.summary: Teachers union head Randi Weingarten and her teachers union allies are desperately trying to manufacture a narrative that Republicans lost ground in the midterms because of school choice. She said that "voters across the nation rejected the defunding of schools and the far-right’s culture wars and privatization agenda." The claim collapses under basic evidence. Texas Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa took aim at school choice during her victory speech on election night when she said, "We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam." Texas Democrats have already filed proposals to rip away scholarships from more than 100,000 mostly low-income kids right after campaigning on affordability. Most of the 10 Democrat Senate cosponsors either attended private school or sent their own children there. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR Demand for the program itself undercuts any claim of backlash. More than 274,000 students applied for Texas Education Freedom Accounts in the first year, with over 100,000 funded. Tens of thousands of families are on a waitlist after available funding ran out. NBC exit polling from 2022 and 2026 shows Abbott received about the same percentage of the rural vote each election, between 64 and 66%. Gov. Greg Abbott held steady with rural voters in Texas even as his overall share of the vote shifted nine points to the left amid a nationwide blue wave. DAN PATRICK CONCEDES TEXAS ‘TURNED PURPLE’ AFTER DEMOCRATS’ HISTORIC BLUE WAVE If rural voters had turned on Abbott because of school choice, exit polling would have shown him losing ground with them. Yet he held steady with those families. Education ranked near the bottom of voters’ top issues, well behind the economy and immigration. BLUE WAVE MEETS BALLOT BOX SURPRISES AS VOTERS SPLIT ON ABORTION, VOTER ID AND BILLIONAIRE TAXES And although more than 20 seats flipped from Republican to Democrat in the Texas House overall, only one of those flips occurred in the 30 most rural districts, which remained heavily Republican. Texas voters rejected nearly $7 billion – about 85% of the total dollars considered on the ballot – in more money for the public school system this month. Texas voters overwhelmingly approved, 79.4% to a mere 20.6%, a ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption from school district property taxes just last year. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES Voters chose to reduce local taxes and associated revenue for public schools by a huge margin, undercutting any claim that they were clamoring for more money to put into the government school system or punishing Republicans over education policy. A University of Texas at Austin poll conducted in October showed voters equally trusted the two gubernatorial candidates on public education. Democrats have historically held a double-digit advantage on the issue of education, so Hinojosa having a zero-point advantage suggests her education platform did not resonate with voters. A 2024 University of Houston poll showed 69% of Texas voters supported universal education savings accounts. University of Texas at Tyler polling also showed 60% support for school choice in 2023. PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS Eighty-eight percent of Texas Republican primary voters supported school choice on the 2022 ballot, and overall support was about the same for large and small counties. Republican primary voters overwhelmingly backed school-choice candidates in recent elections. In one example, in 2024, anti-school-choice incumbent Glenn Rogers lost his primary by 27 points. The Dallas Morning News pushed propaganda from the teachers union by running an op-ed by "longtime Republican" Suzanne Bellsnyder that created a narrative that rural Republicans were embracing Hinojosa. The paper later added a note clarifying editors were not aware that Suzanne Bellsnyder’s firm was paid $57,000 by the Hinojosa campaign, and they would not have published the piece if they had known. The newspaper still refused to pull down the article entirely. TEACHERS UNION SPENT NEARLY $8M TO CRUSH SCHOOL CHOICE, BIOLOGICAL SPORTS MEASURES, REPORT FINDS The argument that school choice hurts rural communities fails on the merits. As school choice expands and brings more options to rural areas, families will have the choice to attend their district school. But they will no longer be resigned to it if the school is a poor fit. At the same time, competition is a rising tide that lifts all boats and improves public schools. The oldest voucher programs in the country started in Maine and Vermont in the late 1800s specifically for kids in rural areas that did not have public schools. Over 150 years ago, these states figured out that not having a lot of options is a good reason to expand education opportunities, not restrict them. Those programs remain on the books today. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Mississippi and Alaska both flipped Senate seats to Democrats even though neither has a universal school-choice program. The leftward movement was national. If anything, the evidence suggests Hinojosa might have won by more if she had sided with parents and supported school choice. School choice did not cost Abbott his election. But it might cost those now in power theirs in the future if they rip scholarships away from families who already have them. Once parents get school choice, they fight hard to keep it. items.originalTitle: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
items.author: Jonquilyn Hill
items.title: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
items.summary: “When we're playing with a toy, we're often doing something we've never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen,” Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, tells Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast. | Chen Siyumeng/Xinhua via Getty Images Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends. We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store. There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine. What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids. It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend. This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children. There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults. According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play. But our society deeply misunderstands that. We’ve slowly started to take play away as we grow up, and yet that drive is still there.” So what does play actually do for our brains, and how can we add the playfulness of childhood back into our adult lives? We answer that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sundstrom, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545. Adult consumers are making up the lion’s share of the toy industry now. What is happening in our adult brains when we play with toys? Neuroplasticity means that our brains can adapt across our entire lifespan. Some of the similar benefits that children have with playing with toys, we actually still have as adults. The primary reason is because of the hand-brain connection, which is essentially a two-way neurological highway. When we do fine motor movement while we’re playing with toys, it stimulates the brain regions that are responsible for our cognitive function, our emotion, and our focus. It activates these deep neural networks that go completely unused when we’re engaging in, say, passive screen time. When we’re playing with a toy, we’re often doing something we’ve never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen. That is actually stimulating new neural pathways in our brain that support our long-term cognitive health. The second big one is our amygdala, which is a key part of our emotional processing center in our brain, is relaxed in the state of play. A lot of us live in a stress response right now. Social media doesn’t really take us out of that stress response. It often leaves us feeling more stressed out or drained when we’re done. I absolutely have experienced that. But that’s not the case with the toys. When we engage in this play state with toys, our amygdala actually calms down. The amygdala is responsible for our stress response. So our stress, our anxiety, our emotional defensiveness are significantly reduced, and we enter that restorative state, which for a lot of us is really hard to access on the day-to-day. Toys are a pathway to helping us access that more relaxed emotional state based on the reactivity of our amygdala. When do we start being told that we’re too old for toys? What do we lose when we accept that? Sadly, I think we’re being told that we’re too old for toys starting quite early. Specifically, when we hit the teenage years, a lot of play is replaced with, “If this doesn’t have an immediate purpose for my future career, it’s not worth the time.” That free space to experiment, say, with Lego and even with collections and other things that stimulate our imagination and allow us to enter this world between imagination and reality, starts to slowly dwindle out, almost imperceptibly. Parents think that they’re doing their children a service by replacing that free play time with structured sports or structured activities. Unfortunately, what happens is, slowly, the intrinsic motivation to do something gets replaced with extrinsic motivation, which very quickly leads to burnout. It sounds like when we stop playing with toys, that’s when the optimization culture kicks in. Exactly. We see playing with toys as extra, as a hobby, as something that doesn’t have an immediate purpose toward helping us achieve whatever our goals are. And yet paradoxically, it’s one of the most productive things we can do. One of the things that I like to ask people is, “Where are you when you get your best ideas?” Now, the shower is the most common answer, but the second most common answer is when they’re playing with toys. You know how no one answers that question? “When I’m at my desk at 10 am answering emails.” The creative mind flourishes in the space in between, and the space in between is the time that is spent playing with toys. But until people see it like that, it becomes really hard to fit into the hustle culture and the grind of the daily schedule. How do we relearn how to play? “Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference.” The first step is to think back on our earliest memories of playing, because play is who we were before the world told us who we have to be. The second, which is a derivative of that, is understanding your own play style. For some people, building a Lego set is going to be totally playful. For other people it’s going to be a puzzle or it’s going to be a game night with a board game or a sports league. And third, this is not about adding more to our plate. Nobody has time for that. That’s so funny. My first thought is, “I need to put play on my to-do list.” And that is totally contradictory to the purpose of play! Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference. You can put play objects and toys in visible places around your environment so that you reach for that instead of your phone. If you just crack the door open a little bit with those micro moments of play in your routine, your brain will automatically enjoy it and start looking for more opportunities to play. Just start really small and know that that’s enough. What do you think the world looks like when adults embrace that playful spirit more? The world looks more joyful. This isn’t all sunshine and rainbows, and play doesn’t take away from the hard things that it means to be human. Play is a healthy way to express those challenges and to express the full range of emotions. Play can look mellow and play can look lower-energy, but what it looks like is humans honoring what it means to be human and feeling more connected with your authentic self. When we’re more connected with our authentic self, we’re more easily able to connect with the people around us and establish meaningful relationships. So I see this as a tool for societal flourishing, specifically in a technologically dominated world.
