items.originalTitle: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
items.author: Pete Kiehart / Bloomberg / Getty
items.title: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
items.summary: P resident Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have a ready answer to the question of how the nine-month conflict with Iran has gone: We won . But the administration has done just about everything in its power to obstruct scrutiny of that dubious claim, hiding from the public the full cost of the operation in both lives and money. When Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat from Connecticut, headed to the Persian Gulf last month, he made what would once have been considered a routine request to visit Al Udeid, the giant U.S. air base outside the capital of Qatar that is home to the regional headquarters of Central Command. Typically, the base is home to 10,000 troops and more than 100 aircraft. Iran pounded it with air strikes soon after Trump launched the Iran war in February, but the conflict was largely paused when Murphy showed up. Murphy sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, which must decide how the government spends taxpayer money. It’s the committee that has to sign off on expected funding requests to repair Al Udeid and other bases hit by Iranian attacks, as well as the extra $67 billion the administration has sought for war costs. Murphy requested a tour, a briefing, anything that could help him make an assessment of the damage and cost of repairs. The Pentagon said no. When Republican Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa, an Army veteran who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made her own trip to the Gulf around the same time, the Defense Department told her that she would not be able to conduct base visits, a person familiar with the matter told me. Ernst’s office did not reply to a request for comment. Behind the rebuffs lies a decision made by Hegseth early in the war to discourage congressional travel to the region. The Pentagon couldn’t ban lawmakers from heading to the Middle East. But Hegseth instructed the Pentagon’s legislative office to “inform the appropriate congressional leadership that DoW support to congressional delegation visits will be unavailable,” according to a March 3 memo I reviewed. (DoW is an acronym for the Department of War, Hegseth’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.) To emphasize the point, the memo added: “No DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.” (U.S. Central Command is in charge of war operations; AOR stands for “area of responsibility.”) Perhaps the edict made sense in the war’s earliest days. But the campaign had already been in limbo for many months by the time Murphy and Ernst made their requests. The policy remains in effect. Senators aren’t the only people being denied access. Early in the war, the U.S. military provided a drumbeat of information about how the war was going. But that information was highly selective: the Defense Department offered a tally of “targets struck” (13,000 in the initial weeks) and the hardware deployed. The Pentagon regularly turned down media requests for more detail, citing “operational security.” And it has allowed only a handful of reporters to embed with troops, far fewer than in previous wars. Hegseth and General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, also held sporadic press conferences at the start of the conflict, during which Hegseth detailed how much of Iran’s military had been destroyed. The secretary insisted that the U.S. military was being transparent and that anyone who thought otherwise was trying to attack the president or was being unpatriotic. (This was after he had severely restricted media access to the Pentagon and vowed to go after purported leaks.) But as the war ground on, the press conferences stopped. Hegseth hadn’t held one since early May until last week, when he used the occasion to argue against an effort to impeach him by a congressman of his own party. [ Read: The last days of the Pentagon press corps ] Although Congress and the public have continued to pose questions that are central to understanding the war, the administration has provided only inadequate answers. What exactly led to a U.S. strike on a school in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war, killing more than 170 civilians? A targeting error was reportedly to blame, but a Centcom report on the incident has not been released, and Hegseth has never addressed the cause. How much damage have Iran’s strikes done to U.S. facilities in the Middle East? What little we know comes largely from photos taken by witnesses that were posted to social media, satellite images (many of them released by Iranian media), and outside estimates. What happened to U.S. citizens and government personnel in the region? We learned details of the hasty evacuation of military families from the giant Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain only when some of the evacuees claimed , months later, that the Pentagon had treated them poorly. What has the war done to the supply of air-defense missiles? The Trump administration has banned some news organizations from the White House, citing their reporting on the dramatic shortfalls, among other factors. How many times has Iran hit U.S. bases in the region? Some significant attacks have not been disclosed, including missile strikes on the air command center at Al Udeid or on a U.S. ship in the Strait of Hormuz, both of which were later reported by the media. What were the circumstances that caused the deaths of 23 American service members and injuries to more than 850 others? And is that casualty count even accurate? Trump is now considering resuming strikes on Iran in an attempt to head off the reconstitution of its nuclear and missile programs, despite the strong signal of disapproval that voters sent in the midterms. Plans for a renewed escalation are on his desk, and he has told Vice President Vance not to make any overtures to Tehran, saying the time for diplomacy is over. The information vacuum of the last nine months means that even as the president contemplates taking the nation back into conflict, we have a limited picture of what has already happened. H egseth’s disdain for the press and for engaging with Congress began long before the war. Before his 2025 confirmation hearings, he declined to hold customary meetings with most Democratic senators on the Senate Armed Services Committee. Once in office, he barred even very senior Pentagon officials from engaging Congress without authorization. Pentagon officials have provided a series of classified briefings on the Iran war for lawmakers. U.S. Central Command told me that it has engaged with them roughly 60 times this year, through testimony, briefings, and phone calls. But the flow of information has been restricted to partisan allies. Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota this week criticized the Pentagon for excluding Democrats from classified briefings about threats while defense officials are asking Congress for new funding. The same has happened in the House. “Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that, if they’re not even invited in to hear the information in the first place,” Rounds told Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to lead the Navy. Military officials have also limited disclosures to official government watchdogs. In a September report on the costs of the war, the Congressional Budget Office—Capitol Hill’s resident bean counter—was forced to piece together information, largely from public reporting, to estimate the value of lost equipment (at least $1.9 billion, it concluded) because the Pentagon didn’t respond to its requests for information. Pentagon officials have estimated the cost of the war’s operations and replacement of munitions at about $48 billion as of mid-November, but many people believe that the full tally is far higher. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, and several Senate colleagues complained last month that the Pentagon provided only a classified cost estimate that they were unable to share with the public. The State Department had no such qualms and disclosed its own estimate for the repair of U.S. diplomatic facilities in the region: about $184 million through the end of June. [ Read: How the U.S. squandered its strategic advantage ] The Pentagon has said it can’t provide a cost estimate for the damage because officials haven’t decided what and where to rebuild. A spokesperson for the Pentagon declined to provide an on-the-record comment for this story. Murphy told me he has been trying to fill in some of the information gaps. “How on earth could we make decisions that we are empowered by the Constitution to make about whether we fund war if we can’t see it?” he said during an event last month. Of course, there is always an element of political grandstanding to lawmaker trips. But lawmakers have asserted their prerogative to make fact-finding missions as part of the U.S. system of checks and balances. Some congressional staff members told me they understood the Pentagon would want to avoid diverting resources during an active fight. And one former Biden administration official told me that, early in the Ukraine war, the administration at times barred lawmakers from traveling to Kyiv. But the Pentagon ultimately relaxed the ban and made security arrangements to support lawmakers’ visits, even though the Ukraine war, unlike the Iran war, is not one where the U.S. has been a direct participant. Robert Wilkie, who served as the Pentagon’s top legislative-affairs official during the Iraq War, told me that Hegseth’s blanket ban on access for lawmakers marked a departure from a practice that dated to at least World War II. Military leaders may not have always loved the spectacle associated with those visits, but they knew such trips were an essential part of congressional oversight. They’re also a tool the military uses to persuade lawmakers to favor bigger budgets. As Wilkie put it, referring to the gun-slinging action hero of the 20th century: “The commanders understand that it’s ‘No bucks, no Buck Rogers.’” T he Pentagon’s disclosures about the war’s toll on military personnel have been limited and obscured by bureaucratic choices. A Pentagon-run website lists the deaths and injuries of service members for all major U.S. conflicts going back to World War I. But in July, four deaths and dozens of injuries disappeared from its totals for Operation Epic Fury, the military’s name for the Iran war. At first, the Pentagon blamed a “data disruption” and said that there was no effort to mask the true toll. Days later, the website was updated with a new category: “Overseas Operations.” The deaths and injuries that had disappeared reemerged under the new listing. Officials pointed to a letter Trump had sent to Congress claiming a new conflict with Iran had started on July 7. Some of the service members wounded in Iranian attacks have said that the military downplayed or dismissed their injuries. The Defense Department’s division of casualties into two categories makes it harder for the public to see the total toll. The Pentagon has defended the system’s accuracy despite what it has described as “website glitches.” [ Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] Hegseth has at times appeared dismissive of casualties. A drone attack in the opening days of the war killed six troops at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. When reporters sought details, Hegseth accused the press of hyping the loss. “When a few drones get through or tragic things happen, it’s front-page news,” he told reporters at a news conference on March 4. “The press only wants to make the president look bad.” Congress’s new Democratic leaders can be expected to push the Pentagon on its handling of casualties when they take over early next year. Hegseth and Trump may want to portray the war as a victory already in hand. But the defense secretary still needs lawmakers on at least one front: money. In a video statement before the planned impeachment vote, Hegseth included a pitch for the administration’s $1.5 trillion military budget request and for tens of billions more to cover the already-sunk costs of the Iran war—whatever those really are.

items.originalTitle: A Movie About What Happens When the Party’s Over
items.author: A24
items.title: A Movie About What Happens When the Party’s Over
items.summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Fiza Kuzhiyil, an assistant editor on the Community team who works on Rabbithole , the magazine’s daily trivia game. Fiza has dedicated her year to a timeless read: Anna Karenina . She also enjoys the movie Club Kid , playing Overcooked 2 with her brother, and visiting the Rothko Chapel when she goes home to Houston. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The Culture Survey The last thing that made me cry: Club Kid —a touching story about what happens when the party is over. This film is the grown-up version of the only Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson movie I have ever seen: the 2007 Disney classic (at least in my household) The Game Plan . Rather than depicting the queer party scene as a hedonistic trap, Club Kid celebrates it as a source of real joy and community. This film feels like the Uber ride home after a party, so how could I—someone who cries at the end of a hangout because I’m so grateful for my friends—not leave in tears? The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Club Kid . If you’re as online as I am, you’ll roll your eyes at the meme-speak, but it’s impossible not to laugh when you get the references—the kind that make you feel seen, then immediately worried about your screen time. Best novel I’ve recently read: Instead of setting a numerical reading goal this year, a friend and I decided to commit to one great, long classic: Anna Karenina . When people ask me if I’ve read anything good recently, I almost always skip over it, not because it didn’t rank, but because what more is there to say than Anna Karenina is the best novel of all time? I can hardly add to what these 19th-century Russian characters have already described about the emotions that I also know—emotions so familiar, they transcend language. Reading it showed me how everyone who came before me has expressed the same thrills, fears, and heartbreaks that I have. The joy of experiencing this novel comes not from deep revelations of plot, but from immersing yourself in the lives of these characters; or, in Leo Tolstoy’s own words, “Pleasure lies not in discovering truth, but in seeking it.” A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “Oh, What a World,” by Kacey Musgraves is always my reminder to be quiet, listen to the world, and take note of my senses. Its counter in my life is the rhapsodic “Trinidad,” by Geese, which is my reminder to accept the tension buzzing among everything I see, hear, and touch. That being said, my loved ones don’t find it amusing when I let go of these tensions by randomly yelling the lyrics to this song (“THERE’S A BOMB IN MY CAR”). A musical artist who means a lot to me: Lorde’s four-year music-release cycles have aligned perfectly with major chapters of my life. I made a big cross-country move listening to Pure Heroine , spent late nights in high school with Melodrama , emerged from the pandemic bubble with Solar Power , and started my first years out of college with Virgin . I saw her three times on her most recent tour, and each time, she sang and spoke about the same themes many artists do— love, loss, youth, autonomy —but the rawness and precision in her delivery has always affected me a step above the others. A painting, sculpture, or other piece of visual art that I cherish: The Rothko Chapel in Houston, both a nondenominational meditative space and an art exhibition, is the only place of worship I visit regularly. I was lucky to have lived on the same street as the chapel for some time. Whenever I feel disoriented or untethered, a quiet moment with the blackout triptychs feels baptismal. Something I recently revisited: My Beatles album ranking—I was always a Sgt. Pepper girl, but I think I’m entering a Rubber Soul time of my life. A piece of journalism that recently changed my perspective on a topic: Some of my D.C. friends call me the one-woman Houston Department of Tourism—which is to say that I won’t shut up about Houston or Texas. Inevitably, non-Texans ask me about Buc-ee’s, the behemoth of a gas station. For a while, its outsize Texas-ness felt like a point of cultural pride; I liked being asked about it. But Forrest Wilder’s essay in The Baffler about the company’s water-rights battles and the cost taxpayers incur for its expansion changed the way I felt about letting Buc-ee’s represent me or my state. I may still wear my beaver-printed running shorts, but I think differently about allowing a corporation to serve as a cultural marker. My favorite way of wasting time on my phone: I am delighted by the recent obsession with browser games among my friends. Krillion rewards obscure and rare answers with more points, which, frankly, panders well to my uniqueness complex. I also spend too much time playing Catfishing , but I consider it “research” for the trivia questions I write for The Atlantic ’s Rabbithole game (shameless plug). Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: Overcooked 2 . I don’t know if I’d call the game itself delightful, because I often take breaks so as to not get too angry, but I am delighted by how my little brother and I are forced to communicate better when we play it. I once preferred the soothing music and satisfying chopping of Cooking Mama on Nintendo DS, but my brother put me on to the new wave of cooking games: cooperative, stressful, and fast-paced. A major perk of our large sibling age gap is that our daily functions rarely overlap, so we have few reasons to get mad at each other. But through Overcooked , we have finally found a way. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : Ian Bogost: What on earth is going on? The real reason Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond Maxwell Taylor Kennedy: Trump’s arch must be stopped. The Week Ahead Focker-in-Law , a new installment in the Meet the Parents comedy franchise, starring Robert De Niro and Ariana Grande (in theaters Wednesday) Blade Runner 2099 , a sci-fi series set in the dystopian world of the Blade Runner 2049 film, 50 years later (streaming Wednesday on Prime Video) Long Wave , a novel by Daisy Johnson about three generations of women and the family secrets that begin to unravel when a toddler is found alone on a remote island (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic The Least Productive Day of the Year By Sophia Nguyen Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out. She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. “I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,” Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait. Read the full article. More in Culture Anna Holmes: ChatGPT analyzed 32,245 of my text messages. items.originalTitle: Independent audit suggests several changes to Wisconsin school district report cards
items.author: Corrinne Hess / WPR
items.title: Independent audit suggests several changes to Wisconsin school district report cards
items.summary: Reading Time: 3 minutes An independent audit is calling for changes in Wisconsin’s school report cards, saying they fall short of providing school performance information required by statute. The Legislative Audit Bureau, or LAB, issued a 146-page report Friday reviewing school report cards from 2022 through 2025 for public, charter and private schools. The audit was commissioned by the Republican-led Joint Legislative Audit Committee in February 2025 after DPI changed how the report cards are scored. LAB made 13 recommendations to DPI and suggested the department report to the Joint Legislative Audit Committee by March 30, 2027 on efforts to implement all of the recommendations. After receiving the report, Sen. Eric Wimberger, R-Gillett, and Rep. Robert Wittke, R-Caledonia, who chair the audit committee, said “DPI unilaterally turned school report cards into an untrustworthy sham.” “Accountability is not optional,” Wittke said in a statement. “The Department of Public Instruction must demonstrate that it is putting Wisconsin students, families, and schools ahead of politics and bureaucracy.” State Superintendent Jill Underly said it is “notable” that the audit is being released the same week school district report cards were issued after months of silence from LAB. “Let’s be clear: Our job at the DPI is to do what’s best for Wisconsin’s kids and families. The Legislative Audit Bureau’s job is to conduct objective, fact-based audits, and not play politics,” Underly said in a statement. “This audit offers nothing new,” Underly continued. “The DPI has been transparent throughout this process, participated in multiple public legislative hearings on these issues, and repeatedly answered questions about our work. Instead of providing meaningful new information and recommendations, the audit makes factually incorrect assertions, goes beyond the scope of its review, and reads like a continuation of last legislative session’s partisan political theater rather than a review conducted in good faith.” Lowest performing schools not receiving intervention On Tuesday, 95% of Wisconsin public school districts were ranked with three, four or five stars. Those rankings reflect meeting, exceeding or significantly exceeding expectations. School report cards look at four priority areas for three school years: achievement, growth, target group outcomes and on-track to graduation. At the same time, test scores released in October showed 48% of students in grades three through 11 were proficient or above in reading while about 49% were proficient or above in math. Part of the reason for this discrepancy is DPI weighs student achievement and growth more than student performance in calculating overall scores in low income districts. This methodology was approved by a GOP-led state Legislature and signed into law by former Gov. Scott Walker. Critics of the state report card say methodology makes it impossible for parents to make apples-to-apples comparisons between districts across the state. In 2021, a bill was introduced that would have given all four priority areas equal weight. Gov. Tony Evers vetoed the bill. In his veto message, Evers said he objected to the Legislature’s “continued efforts to politicize our schools and our classrooms.” Criticism for state report cards grew louder in 2024, when DPI rolled out new testing standards and updated the “cut scores ,” which determine where the schools and districts fall on the star scale. At the time, Underly said the updates were needed to keep pace with changes to performance measures. Republicans and outside conservative groups, including the Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty and Institute for Reforming Government, have continued to argue the changes lowered standards. Wimberger said the audit shows DPI “circumvented statutes and lowered cut scores so that otherwise failing schools appear to be on track.” While the audit released Friday does not specifically say that DPI lowered standards, it found that DPI’s assessment process is not creating conditions for intervention when schools are meeting minimal performance standards. The percentage of schools meeting, exceeding, or significantly exceeding expectations increased from school year 2022-2023 to school year 2024-2025, and the percentage of schools meeting few expectations or failing to meet expectations decreased from school year 2022-2023 to school year 2024-2025, according to the audit. The school performance category assigned to most schools and school districts did not change from school year 2023-2024 to school year 2024-2025. However, 20.2% of schools and 21% of school districts moved up one school performance category during that time, the audit found. The audit also found DPI should have released written policies to all stakeholders about testing changes. The audit says the department did not solicit feedback broadly from educators or members of the public before making changes. “Although DPI indicated it received informal feedback from stakeholders about changing assessment cut scores through ad hoc conversations and discussions during meetings and presentations, DPI was unable to provide documentation of the feedback it received or how it used the feedback to inform the changes it made,” the audit found. This story was originally published by WPR . items.originalTitle: By electing Scott Colom, Mississippi has done what most other states have not
items.author: Bobby Harrison
items.title: By electing Scott Colom, Mississippi has done what most other states have not
items.summary: It has been difficult in recent days to tune to a television news show and not see Scott Colom or at least people talking about Scott Colom. He has become sort of a national sensation – the next big thing for political nerds and perhaps even for many who take a more casual interest in politics. In the Nov. 3 midterm election, Colom, a Democratic district attorney from the Lowndes County area, upset Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black person elected through popular vote to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi. The watershed election has to be viewed against the historical backdrop of Mississippi’s sordid racist history. Regardless of one’s political views, it could be argued that Colom’s victory provides Mississippi a good dose of needed redemption. Mississippi is only the third state from the footprint of the old Confederacy – and all of the lingering segregation and racism that followed the downfall of the Confederacy – to have elected a Black person to the United States Senate. South Carolina elected Republican Tim Scott in 2012, and Georgia elected Democrat Raphael Warnock in 2020. Perhaps more impressive in terms of Colom’s accomplishment is that only nine Black people before this year have ever been elected via popular vote to the United States Senate. Come January, Colom will join five other Black senators, including the aforementioned fellow Southerners, Warnock and Scott. Being sworn in with Colom will be Juliana Stratton, the second Black woman elected to the Senate from Illinois and the fifth Black woman ever elected to the upper chamber of Congress. Illinois has elected the most Black senators – three – and had another who was appointed to succeed Barack Obama after he was elected president. Only nine states – California, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, South Carolina and now Mississippi – have elected Black senators. It is worth noting that a Mississippi native, Laphonza Butler , was appointed to fill one of California’s U.S. Senate seats in 2023 after the death of Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Butler service until December 2024 and did not seek election to the post. It is also worth noting that Mississippi was the only state after the Civil War during Reconstruction to have Black citizens serve in the U.S. Senate – Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce . They were selected by the state Legislature instead of via popular vote. Again, regardless of one’s politics, it is fair to say Mississippi is a trendsetter in this particular instance. But an important question for us here in Mississippi is: What took us so long to elect a Black person to a statewide office? Before Colom, Mississippi had not elected a Black person to statewide office since Reconstruction, despite currently having the largest percentage of Black residents in the country – around 38%. Mississippi has had some Black candidates get relatively close in statewide election efforts. In the 2003 race for state treasurer, Democrat Gary Anderson, who was the state fiscal officer under Gov. Ronnie Musgrove, garnered 46.6% of the vote in a losing effort against Republican Tate Reeves, a political unknown running his first campaign. In November 2018, former U.S. Agriculture Commissioner Mike Espy captured 46.4% of the vote in losing a special election to Hyde-Smith, who had been appointed by Gov. Phil Bryant earlier that year to serve temporarily after fellow Republican Thad Cochran retired. Hyde-Smith and Espy competed to fill the remaining years of Cochran’s term. Two years later when Hyde-Smith was running for a full six-year-term, Espy received 44.1% of the vote in a rematch. It should be pointed out that the 2020 election was a presidential year and the highest vote-total election in the state’s history. In that election, Espy captured nearly 100,000 more votes in a losing effort than Colom received in his recent winning effort. Election turnouts are normally much lower in midterm elections than in presidential elections. Mississippi is one of few states that elect a governor, other statewide offices and state legislators between the presidential and midterm elections. So, next year Mississippi will elect eight statewide officials, including for the open office of governor because Reeves cannot seek a third term. A big question now: Will another Black candidate replicate Scott Colom’s success to win a different statewide office?

items.originalTitle: Make America boring again
items.author: Vic Snyder
items.title: Make America boring again
items.summary: Ben Shapiro , the conservative commentator and movie maker, is not happy with today’s Republican Party and quite disappointed with where Donald Trump’s decisions have taken our country. He has not been reluctant to express his views. But at the end of a recent NPR interview, he was asked what advice he had for Democrats and what advice for Republicans. His answer, he said, was the same for both parties: the American people want normal. My guess is he means normal by the standards of the American people, not elected officials who won or survived an earthquake of an election. Here’s what I think normal looks like: less chaos. We used to call this business climate. Tariffs have a place in modern economies, but during the past two years Trump’s tariff policy has had the stability of a teenager crush. Trade agreements exist to give predictability for businesses, not to be ignored in some moment of anger or bewilderment. Confusion about America’s world leadership, the importance of NATO, and the threat of Russia to Europe and the world contributes to instability internationally. Second, the American people want a Congress that goes to work and works for them. Rep Jim Jordan ’s apparent belligerent intent as the new minority leader misses the potentially important role that minority members can play in shaping legislation. And Rep. Robert Garcia ’s repeated school-ground threat to his oversight targets to “lawyer up” misses several realities. The Trump family was born lawyered up, and does anyone doubt the likelihood that Trump’s pardons prior to leaving office will be broad? The American people want oversight that makes us a better country by improving law, improving transparency, and stopping corruption. Criminal referrals are important in congressional oversight, but Americans don’t want shows, particularly if they seem to be connected with campaign fundraising. I am tired of Rep Garcia’s fundraising requests. Third, how about a list of priorities that warrant oversight and change? Here’s a few. Tens of thousands of Americans are still recovering from natural disasters. Disasters are always in our future. What is the role of FEMA now and what will it be going forward? Can we return to a FEMA that has the confidence of the American people like we did with Arkansas’ James Lee Witt? For many areas of the country businesses depend on a strong tourist economy connected to our national parks and public lands. What is happening to the National Park System? Where is the funding going? Why is staffing inadequate? Have funds been diverted to weird projects in Washington, D.C.? With Democrats now in control, let’s find out the status of medical research, research that improves our health and drives a chunk of our economy. What have we lost and how much can be recovered from DOGE amateur-hour cuts? Have researchers been so intimidated they have been reluctant to talk candidly about the impact of funding cuts and what it means for the research infrastructure and the health of Americans? Why are health insurance rates increasing, and what can be done about it? Americans need financial stability for themselves, their children, and their small businesses. A strong rural America depends on strong rural hospitals with financial predictability. Normal governing should not fill every day with breaking news. It is work. I am confident there are many representatives and senators, new and old, many not in the news, feeling their own excitement at the prospect of productivity for America. And in America, productivity is normal. Let’s get to it.

items.originalTitle: Trump’s USDA changed the rules. Farmers and rural businesses paid the price
items.author: Veronica McFadden
items.title: Trump’s USDA changed the rules. Farmers and rural businesses paid the price
items.summary: This year, I was forced to lay off all five of my employees. My business wasn’t defeated by a competitor or a declining market. It was devastated by a decision from my own government. I founded Sun Grants Consulting in 2023 to help farmers and rural small businesses apply for grants through the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP). We grew to five employees and filed almost 200 applications. In March, USDA announced it would stop processing pending REAP applications and make no further grant awards until new regulations took effect. Applicants who had followed the existing rules would have to start over . Fifty-seven of my clients’ applications were caught in that decision, representing more than $22 million in rural energy investments and more than $9 million in grant awards. Because my firm is paid only when clients win grants, our anticipated revenue from those applications vanished. Congress created REAP in the 2002 farm bill to encourage renewable energy and efficiency investments. It has enjoyed bipartisan support, including reauthorization in the 2018 farm bill President Trump signed. REAP is not a blank check: Farmers and business owners put their own capital at risk, hire private contractors and pay costs the grants do not cover. Then came a second blow. USDA issued a new rule in October that fundamentally changed how future applicants qualify. Farmers and businesses generally must complete projects, pay the bills and document 12 months of energy production or savings before they can even apply. USDA itself concedes “some uncertainty about whether an applicant will receive an award.” USDA has turned an investment incentive into a reimbursement lottery. The businesses most in need of assistance are often least able to gamble their capital on a grant decision a year or more away. Consider Michigan dairy farmer Ron Rusk , whose REAP application I helped prepare. After applying under the previous rules, he invested approximately $86,000 in solar equipment. He sought a grant covering roughly a quarter of the cost. USDA’s March reversal left his pending application in limbo and the October rule terminated his application. The damage extends beyond applicants. The National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition estimates that each REAP grant dollar generates $8.72 in total project spending. That means work for electricians, installers, manufacturers and rural contractors. USDA’s own budget documents say REAP projects give farmers and rural small businesses “new and sustainable income streams.” Yet USDA’s March announcement vowed to end “taxpayer handouts” for renewable energy, and the president’s executive order targets “market distorting subsidies.” The REAP grant is taxable income , and USDA says a farmer can claim it alongside the federal solar tax credit. In October, USDA announced $8 billion in assistance to farmers facing higher fuel costs. Emergency relief may be warranted. But why is helping farmers pay for fuel acceptable while helping them invest in permanently lowering their energy bills is condemned? The administration also invokes farmland protection. USDA research found that solar and wind installations directly occupied less than 0.05% of U.S. farmland in 2020. Protecting productive land matters; making energy grants harder to access for rural businesses is a different matter. There is a political irony, too. Brookings found that about two-thirds of REAP grants went to districts now represented by Republicans; 18 of the 20 districts receiving the most are Republican-held. These policies fall hardest on communities the administration promises to defend. The legal question is serious. Congress instructed USDA to “promote” renewable energy and efficiency for rural businesses, yet the USDA’s new rule itself says the policies behind it direct USDA to “disincentivize solar development on farmland.” An agency cannot rewrite a statute by policy. Farmers understand risk. They face weather, commodity prices and uncertain markets every year. They should not also have to guess whether Washington will change the rules after they invest. A government that claims to champion American business should understand a fundamental business principle: Your word must mean something. Photo from Adobe Stock The roughly 26,000 Vermonters who receive their health insurance through the state employees’ plan will see a 9% increase in their healthcare premiums starting Jan. 1, according to a memo from the Vermont Department Human Resources. This increase matches last year’s 9% raise, which followed steep, double-digit increases between 2023-2025, according to Ted Fisher, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Human Resources. He said that this year’s rates are a hopeful signal that Vermont has “turned the corner on the trend in annual increases for our state employees.” He is hopeful that it means next year could see a “lower or no increase next year.” Still, the state employees’ union has used the announcement as an opportunity to call on the governor to fast track price caps on hospital care for those on the state employee plans. In June, Gov. Phil Scott vetoed the Legislature’s effort to implement this kind of price cap for school employees and Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. “I think the governor needs to really put reforming the healthcare system at the forefront of his agenda,” Steve Howard, executive director of the Vermont State Employees’ Association, the union representing state workers, told VTDigger. Though Vermont is in the process of putting price caps on hospital prices for all commercial health insurance in the state, the union is urging Scott to sign an executive order to implement these lower prices tied to a benchmarked price of what Medicare pays for the service for state employees. Montana established this type of reference-based pricing for its state employees’ health plans in 2016, but has since sunset it . Oklahoma, South Carolina , West Virginia and eight other states have some version of the price caps for public employee health plans. Vermont is unique among states in its emphasis on price caps across the entire commercial market . READ MORE Scott supports the price caps for all payers, not just a subset of insurance plans, his spokesperson Amanda Wheeler told VTDigger, adding that the governor signed the broad reference-based pricing plan into law. It’s the same reasoning he gave for vetoing this spring’s attempt to fast-track the plan first for public schools’ and marketplace plans. “Implementing it for just one subset of the insurance market would mean other Vermonters would be excluded from those affordability gains, while adding further complexity, inequity, and cost to an already complicated healthcare system,” Wheeler wrote in an email. A 2024 report by the independent healthcare regulator that was ultimately tasked with implementing Vermont’s reference based pricing plan, analyzed the impact a price cap for hospital charges could have on public school employees’ and state employees’ healthcare plans. They found that if the state kept hospital charges for those plans at two times Medicare rates — rather than the status quo of an average 289% of Medicare’s charges — the state could have prevented $400 million of claims payments during the five-year study period. In 2022 alone, the cap could have cut $79 million. Health insurance, broadly, is a measure of the cost of services times the number of services used. Less costly hospital claims means the insurer needs to collect less in premiums to cover them, which means the state would pay less to cover those premiums. For the VSEA plans, the state covers 80% of employees’ premiums. In 2027, the least expensive plans available to state employees have a monthly price tag of $747 for an individual, $1,494 for two people and $2,054 for a family of three or more. “That eats into people’s wages at a time when — because of the president’s tariffs and the economy and the price of gas and the war in Iran and all that stuff — it’s harder and harder for state employees to make ends meet,” Howard said. The increase comes as other insurance groups across Vermont are starting to see the impacts of efforts to lower costs. In August, plans sold on the state’s Affordable Care Act exchange received some of the smallest increases they’ve ever had. That’s due to reduced hospital budgets, reductions in BlueCross BlueShield’s 2026 contract with the state’s largest hospital network, and a 2025 law that capped the cost of some expensive drugs. The same forces influenced Vermont public school employees’ health insurance plans , which expect to see some of the smallest premium increases in more than a decade. Fisher, with the state’s human resources department, said that the state employees’ plans are on track to follow those trends. Before the pandemic, the plans had very small annual increases, he said, but following it, they saw a “spike” in claims and utilization — which is not uncommon as many people went without optional care during the height of COVID-19. That spike pushed the state employee medical fund into a deficit, he said, which $18.5 million of FY25 state general funds have worked to stabilize. This year’s rates seek to do the same kind of stabilization. “As a result of this money and utilization rates stabilizing, we anticipate the fund being in surplus by the end of FY28 (barring unforeseen economic/healthcare factors),” Fisher added. Patrick Sellers indicted on 4 counts of wire fraud (WBRC) A federal grand jury has indicted Alabama state Rep. Patrick Sellers on four counts of wire fraud, accusing him of fraudulently getting more than $240,000 in COVID-19 relief money and using it for his own personal benefit. The charges against Sellers, a Democrat from Pleasant Grove, are for actions taken before he won his seat representing House District 57 in 2022. He has pleaded not guilty. WBRC also discussed how the indictment could affect Sellers in his role as representative. Alabama Public Library Service Board installs new chair, seeks new director (Alabama Reflector) The Alabama Public Library Service Board on Thursday elected Amy Minton, a board member who helped lead efforts to restrict library materials for minors, as its new chair. She will replace John Wahl, recently elected Alabama lieutenant governor. It also voted to post the library director’s position after the current director was given an unsatisfactory rating by four of the seven members. She has not been terminated at this time. The new initiative is the product of a partnership between Autism Support of Alabama and the Transportation Security Administration. Birmingham chef and artist goes to Washington to celebrate African American Sunday supper tradition (WBHM) In many African American homes, the Sunday supper is a cornerstone of family life. It’s a time to reconnect and to share food that reflects history, faith and community. Birmingham chef and artist Roscoe Hall helped showcase this tradition during an event at the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., earlier this year. As a gospel and roots music choir from Arkansas sang, Hall prepared food in a demonstration kitchen atop a stage as part of a Smithsonian Folklife Festival series that explores the intersection of food and music in communities across the country.
